frames.title: Something is coming. We have one year of physics to figure out what.
frames.body:
This course follows a single object — a near‑Earth asteroid called 2026‑XJ — from the day it's detected to the day we can finally say what it will do. Every unit of physics answers one more piece of that puzzle.

A new object, 2026‑XJ, has been detected on an approach toward Earth's neighborhood.

frames.title: A year of physics, one question at a time
frames.body:
Most courses teach motion, then forces, then energy, as separate chapters. Here each one shows up because the asteroid story needs it. You learn momentum because you have to know whether a spacecraft could push the asteroid.

Unit 1 predicts where it's going, assuming it moves in a straight line. It doesn't — gravity bends it. That gap is Unit 2. Each unit ends by naming what it still can't answer.

frames.title: Some questions need a number. Others need an arrow.
frames.body:
Physics keeps two kinds of quantities on purpose. Scalars answer how much. Vectors answer how much, and which way. Neither is "more correct" — the trick is knowing which question you're asking.

A runner finishes one 400 m lap of the track in 60 s and stops exactly where she started.

frames.title: Because directions add, cancel, and split
frames.body:
If scalars are simpler, why does almost every law of mechanics use vectors? Because the world does things scalars can't describe.

Walk 5 m east, then 5 m west. Distance says 10 m; you're standing where you started. Two forces of 100 N on a rope in a tug‑of‑war can produce zero motion. Only arrows can add up to nothing.

frames.title: Direction isn't always information
frames.body:
Vectors carry more, but more isn't free. When the physics genuinely doesn't depend on direction, the scalar is not a shortcut — it's the honest answer, and it makes the math simpler.

Squaring erases the sign. A ball thrown up at 10 m/s and one thrown down at 10 m/s have identical kinetic energy. Energy bookkeeping is scalar — that's what makes it so powerful.

frames.title: Before you can explain motion, you have to describe it.
frames.body:
Kinematics is the language physics uses to say where something is, how fast it's moving, and how that's changing — without yet asking why. Every law you'll learn this year is written in that language.

A car is doing 12 m/s when the light turns red. The driver brakes, slowing steadily at 1.5 m/s².

frames.title: Four quantities, one variable underneath
frames.body:
Kinematics (from the Greek kinēma, "movement") is the geometry of motion. It builds a chain: position is where you are; velocity is how position changes; acceleration is how velocity changes. Each one is the rate of change of the one before it, and time is the thread running through all of them.

Where the object is, measured from an origin you choose. Displacement Δx = xf − xi is the change — a vector, not the distance walked.

frames.title: Describing vs. explaining
frames.body: Classical mechanics splits into two halves. Kinematics answers how things move. Dynamics answers why — it brings in mass and force. Newton's second law, F = ma, is the bridge: the a on the right side is a kinematic quantity.

frames.title: Three reasons, one historical and two logical
frames.body:
For 2,000 years, Aristotle's physics tried to explain motion by purpose. Galileo (c. 1600) changed the question: instead of asking why a ball rolls, he timed it down a ramp and found distance grew with time squared. Measuring first, explaining second — that shift is the scientific method, and kinematics is where it happened.

Newton's laws are statements about acceleration. Momentum is m·v. Kinetic energy is ½mv². Angular velocity, wave speed, orbital period — all are kinematic ideas wearing new clothes. Define x, v, a precisely once, and every later chapter can build on them instead of redefining them.

frames.title: Velocity is how fast position changes. Acceleration is how fast velocity changes.
frames.body:
The derivative is the tool that turns "how fast is this changing?" into a number — at a single instant, not averaged over a trip. Apply it once to position and you get velocity. Apply it again and you get acceleration.

Your car's odometer shows how far you've gone. The speedometer shows how fast you're going right now.

frames.title: Four things the slopes tell you

Wherever x–t has a peak or valley, its tangent is flat, so v = 0. Try the ball toss: at the top, v–t crosses zero.

frames.title: A number without a unit isn't a measurement. It's a guess.
frames.body:
Every quantity in physics is a number times a unit, and every unit is built from a handful of basic dimensions. Learn to read them and equations start telling you what they mean before you calculate anything.

NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter arrived after a nine‑month flight — and vanished into the Martian atmosphere.

frames.title: Three dimensions build all of mechanics
frames.body:
A dimension is the kind of thing you're measuring — length, mass, time. A unit is the agreed‑on amount of it you count with — meters, kilograms, seconds. Mechanics needs only three dimensions. Everything else — speed, force, energy, pressure — is a combination of them.

How far. Defined today by the distance light travels in 1/299 792 458 s — so a meter is the same in every lab on Earth.

frames.title: Every derived unit is a recipe
frames.body: A base unit is defined directly: m, kg, s. A derived unit is a product of powers of base units — nothing more. Some get their own name (newton, joule, watt) because we use them constantly, but the name is a nickname for the recipe. Set the exponents and see what you've built.

frames.title: The mechanics toolkit
frames.body:
Twelve quantities cover almost every problem this year. Learn the base‑unit recipe for each — it's what lets you check your work by inspection.

Notice the pattern: newton, joule, watt and pascal are all just kg·m·s combinations that earned a nickname. If you forget one, rebuild it from a formula you trust — F = ma gives kg·m/s² every time.

frames.title: Units aren't bookkeeping. They're physics.
frames.body:
"The car is going 30" is not information. 30 m/s is highway speed; 30 km/h is a school zone. The Mars orbiter was lost by people who all had the right numbers.

You can't set a length equal to a time, or add a force to an energy. This rule — dimensional homogeneity — lets you reject a wrong formula in ten seconds, before you touch a calculator.
